extracted.intended_audience: USPTO design patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents, and draftspersons) preparing or prosecuting U.S. design patent applications
extracted.subtask_short: design patent drawing and claim requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Requirements and examiner guidance from the MPEP for drafting, amending, and examining design patent drawings, photographs, claims, and related formalities (views, shading, broken lines, color, new matter, replacements, and prosecution practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual disclosure requirement (drawing or photograph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every design patent application must include either a drawing or a photograph of the claimed design; the drawing or photograph constitutes the entire visual disclosure of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the drawing or photograph constitutes the whole disclosure, it is of utmost importance that the drawing or photograph be clear and complete, and that nothing regarding the design sought to be patented is left to conjecture. An insufficient drawing may be fatal to validity (35 U.S.C. 112(a)) and may negatively affect the effective filing date in a continuing application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with 37 CFR 1.152 and 1.84
rubrics_metrics.description: Design drawings must comply with the requirements of § 1.84 and also with 37 CFR 1.152.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to 37 CFR 1.81-1.88, drawings must follow 37 CFR 1.152: include sufficient views, appropriate surface shading, avoid prohibited uses of broken lines, etc. See MPEP § 1503.02 for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient number of views / adequate disclosure of appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings or photographs should contain a sufficient number of views to disclose the complete appearance of the design claimed (may include front, rear, top, bottom and sides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inherently two-dimensional designs a single plan- or planar-view may suffice (see In re Maatita). Perspective views are suggested for three-dimensional designs and may obviate other views if surfaces are fully disclosed. Views that are merely duplicative or flat with no ornamentation may be omitted if the specification explicitly states so (e.g., mirror-image sides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading requirements and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate and adequate surface shading should be used to show the character or contour of surfaces; surface shading is not required but may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of appropriate surface shading in the drawing as filed may render the design nonenabling and indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b). Solid black surface shading is not permitted except when used to represent the color black as well as color contrast. Oblique line shading must be used to show transparent, translucent, and highly polished/reflective surfaces. Contrast may be shown by line shading in one area and stippling in another. Addition of surface shading after filing may comprise new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines: permitted uses and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines may be used to disclose environmental structure or to define the bounds of the claim, but not to indicate that portions of a design are unimportant or immaterial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed subject matter may be shown in broken lines for illustrating environment; such matter must be described as forming no part of the claimed design. Broken lines may not be used to show hidden planes and surfaces, nor to indicate that a portion is less important. When broken-line boundaries are added by amendment or continuation, they must comply with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Broken-line boundaries other than straight broken lines may constitute new matter (prohibited by 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using broken lines to indicate unimportant features
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines for the purpose of indicating unimportant or immaterial features of the design are not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ornamental design being claimed must be shown in solid lines in the drawing; there are no portions of a claimed design which are immaterial or unimportant. See In re Blum and In re Zahn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to describe broken lines in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When broken lines are used, the specification must explicitly describe their purpose and whether they form part of the claimed design or are environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested statement: '--The broken line showing of [1] is for the purpose of illustrating [2] and forms no part of the claimed design.--' This description should precede the claim in the specification so that the scope of the claim is clear, especially when different broken lines in the same application serve different purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When broken-line environment obscures full-line disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If superimposed broken lines showing environmental structure obscure the full-line disclosure of the claimed design, a separate figure showing the broken lines must be included in addition to the figures showing only claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids obscuring or confusing the visual disclosure of the claimed design and preserves enablement/definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate positions and combined media restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate positions illustrated by full and broken lines in the same view are not permitted. Photographs and ink drawings are not permitted to be combined as formal drawings in one application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must not disclose environmental structure and must be limited to the design claimed for the article. Introducing both photographs and drawings in one application risks inconsistencies and is not allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs: when allowed and quality requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs may be accepted in utility and design patent applications only if photographs are the only practicable medium for illustrating the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the photographs are not of sufficient quality so that all details are reproducible, objections will follow and no application will be issued until acceptable photographs are submitted and approved. Photographs used in lieu of ink drawings must be limited to the design claimed and must not disclose environmental structure (37 CFR 1.84(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Color drawings/photographs: filing, specification language, and sets required
rubrics_metrics.description: Color drawings and color photographs are permitted when filed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.84(a); the specification must include a statement that 'The file of this patent contains at least one drawing/photograph executed in color.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If submitted via USPTO patent electronic filing system, only one set of color drawings/photographs is required; if not submitted electronically, three sets are required. The specification language must be included as the first paragraph of the brief description of the drawings. See 37 CFR 1.84(a)(2) and MPEP § 608.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black-and-white lining for color and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: As an alternative to color drawings, surfaces may be lined with graphic symbols in black-and-white to represent color; when so lined, the specification should state 'The drawing is lined for color.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lining entire surfaces for color may interfere with a clear showing of the design since surface shading cannot be used simultaneously to define contours. Partial lining with a description that the color extends across the entire surface may permit shading elsewhere. Some color disclosures (e.g., multiple shades) cannot be accurately represented by the single drafting symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface treatment subject-matter rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface treatment (indicia, contrasting color or materials, graphic representations, or other ornamentation) must be applied to or embodied in an article of manufacture; surface treatment per se is not proper subject matter for a design patent under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface treatment may be shown in full lines or broken lines (if unclaimed). Disclosure of surface treatment in a drawing or photograph is prima facie evidence the inventor considered it integral to the claimed design. Removing or canceling two-dimensional surface treatment may be permitted if applicant had possession of the underlying configuration at filing; removal of three-dimensional surface treatment that is integral to configuration will introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement drawing sheets and labeling requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrected replacement drawing sheets complying with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to an Office action to avoid abandonment; each replacement sheet must include all figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a figure is canceled, it must be removed and remaining figures renumbered with corresponding changes to descriptions. If all figures on a sheet are canceled, a replacement sheet is not required but an 'Annotated Sheet' showing cancellation must be presented. Each drawing sheet submitted after filing must be labeled in the top margin as either 'Replacement Sheet' or 'New Sheet' pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not label amended drawing figures as 'amended'
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as amended on the replacement sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR 1.121(d) practices: replacement sheets should present the final clean version, not mark-ups labeled 'amended' on the sheet itself; use the amendment/remarks section to explain changes and include an Annotated Sheet where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing correction required prior to appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Any appeal of the design claim must include the correction of the drawings approved by the examiner (Ex parte Bevan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph can be used in a FINAL rejection where an outstanding requirement for a drawing correction has not been satisfied; corrected drawings must be approved before the appeal proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of new matter when preparing new/replacement drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing new or replacement drawings, be careful to avoid introducing new matter; new matter is prohibited by 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 15.48 may be used to notify applicant of the necessity for good drawings. Adding features, shading, boundaries, or broken-line shapes that were not present or clearly supported in the original disclosure may be treated as new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectional views: limited and potentially confusing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sectional views presented solely to show internal construction or functional/mechanical features are unnecessary and may lead to confusion as to the scope of the claimed design; the examiner should object and require cancellation unless the sectional view is needed to clarify external contour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a sectional view is added during prosecution, the examiner must determine whether there is antecedent basis in the original disclosure for material shown in hatching per 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) and MPEP § 608.02. Historical precedent (Ex parte Tucker; Ex parte Kohler; Ex parte Lohman) supports caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim form and single-claim rule for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application may include only a single claim. The single claim should normally be in the formal terms: 'The ornamental design for (the article which embodies the design or to which it is applied) as shown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description of the article in the claim should be consistent in terminology with the title of the invention. More than one claim is neither required nor permitted. When the specification includes an appropriate descriptive statement or modified forms, add 'and described' (i.e., 'as shown and described').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'as shown' vs 'as shown and described' in claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: For proper form under 37 CFR 1.153 (or 1.1025 for international design applications), the claim should read either 'The ornamental design for [article] as shown' or '...as shown and described' when descriptive matter is included in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph templates indicate how to amend claims: include 'I' or 'We' as appropriate, and ensure the title of the article is inserted consistently. Examiner notes instruct inserting '--must be--' or '--has been--' in bracketed amendment language when making examiner amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistencies among views and effect on enablement/definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: When inconsistencies are found among the views, the examiner should object and request that the views be made consistent; if inconsistencies are of such magnitude that the overall appearance is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Asano and Hadco Products precedent. If a reply overcomes a rejection, the examiner must indicate the rejection as withdrawn in the next Office action unless notice of allowability is being issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/nonobviousness search scope for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty and nonobviousness of a design claim must generally be determined by a search in the pertinent design classes, and the search must be extended to mechanical classes encompassing inventions of the same general type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogs and trade journals as well as available foreign patent databases are also to be consulted. The inventive novelty or unobviousness resides in the ornamental shape/configuration or surface ornamentation applied to or embodied in the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte Quayle practice for formal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is patentable under statutory requirements but formal matters still need correction prior to allowance, an Ex parte Quayle action should be sent indicating allowability and identifying necessary corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution on the merits is closed under Quayle practice. A shortened statutory period for reply (TWO (2) MONTHS) is set; extensions may be granted under 37 CFR 1.136 but cannot extend beyond statutory maximum. If a rejection is later given after a Quayle reply, indication of allowability must be withdrawn and prosecution reopened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color submissions and later omission of color
rubrics_metrics.description: If color photographs or color drawings are filed with the original application, color will be considered an integral part of the disclosed and claimed design; omission of color in later filed drawings may be permitted only if the application shows possession of the underlying configuration without color at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Daniels precedent: omission of color later is permitted where underlying configuration was apparent in the original filing. Photographs submitted in lieu of ink drawings must not disclose environmental structure (37 CFR 1.152).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification and authorization for examiner amendments to figure descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant's authorization is required to make an examiner's amendment to the figure descriptions, and certain form paragraphs (e.g., 13.02 and 13.02.01) should be used and preceded appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an extension of time is required for such amendments, different form paragraphs should be used (e.g., 13.02.02). Examiner notes provide bracketed insertion instructions for form paragraph usage.
